item.title: Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
item.description: On August 26, a section of glacier collapsed at an altitude of more than 5,000 metres on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas. The falling ice and rock accelerated down a steep valley at about 50 metres per second, scouring debris and transforming into a high-speed mudslide that slammed into Gyirong Port on the Chinese side just seven minutes later. The force of the flow largely buried and obliterated the border facilities. Hundreds of people, many of them travellers, remain missing on the Chinese... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Alepo resurge de las ruinas: la reconstrucción de la capital económica de Siria
item.description: Alepo, la capital económica de Siria, quedó devastada por los combates entre las fuerzas rebeldes y el régimen entre 2012 y 2016. El terremoto de 2023 también dañó gravemente el casco antiguo. Sin embargo, hoy en día se están llevando a cabo trabajos de reconstrucción, especialmente de los monumentos históricos de la ciudad. ¿Cómo avanza esta titánica labor en la capital económica de Siria? Reportaje de Dana Alboz, Sophie Guignon y Yasser Shahrour para France 24. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.description: Every day, new bodies are recovered in Nepal, but many remain unidentifiable. Several days after the disaster, some are already in an advanced state of decomposition. item.title: Environmental, social and governance investor pressure sometimes causes firms to shift pollution to suppliers
item.description: Investors who evaluate companies using environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria are increasingly expected to act as private regulators, using their influence as stakeholders to pressure firms to act more sustainably. New research published in Strategic Management Journal finds that companies under strong ESG investor pressure generate lower direct emissions. However, they sometimes shift pollution to suppliers, which does not change their combined emissions. The study also found evidence that this outsourcing can be reduced when investors help firms adopt eco-friendly technologies… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Next-gen sensors: Catching water pollution in real time
item.description: Extreme weather events, such as floods, droughts and torrential rains, affect water quality in lakes, rivers and coastal areas. This creates significant challenges for ecosystems and water supplies because pesticides bound in soil can quickly leach into water sources. Now, researchers want to monitor this in a new way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forest floor to treetops, cameras reveal Congo Basin's hidden wildlife
item.description: The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) tropical forests stretch across an extraordinary landscape of rivers, wetlands, savannas and towering trees. But in a forest this vast, biodiversity doesn't exist on a single plane. It climbs into the canopy. It moves between branches and vines, disappears into the understory and travels across the forest floor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trawling threatens vital carbon stores in Scotland's sea lochs
item.description: New research from the University of St Andrews shows that disturbing seabed sediments through trawling could cause significant losses of carbon stored in Scotland's sea lochs. The study, published in Marine Environmental Research, shows that organic carbon stored in seabed sediments can be released into the surrounding seawater when disturbed. This carbon is then more likely to be broken down and ultimately returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tunisia's iconic Sidi Bou Said town added to UNESCO world heritage list
item.description: In Tunisia, UNESCO recognised the town of Sidi Bou Said as a world heritage site this July. The special status may help as it battles erosion, like in the floods this last January, but it will also help boost its lesser known Sufi mystical traditions. item.title: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann
item.description: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying. The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event ; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. item.title: 'Glaciers in Himalayas retreating': Nepal floods triggered by 'glacier collapse & massive landslide'
item.description: Annette Young is pleased to welcome Joseph Shea, Glaciologist and Associate Professor at the University of Northern BC. Shea argues that the catastrophe should be understood as a compound event in which a glacier failure and a massive landslide occurred together. His analysis places the disaster within the broader, well-established transformation of the Himalayas under climate change. As warming changes high-mountain environments, scientists may increasingly need to identify subtle precursors to rare but potentially devastating cascading hazards. Fuente: France 24 - English.
